stem: Which expression gives the number of ways of choosing $r$ objects from $n$ distinct objects when order does not matter?

options.rationale: Correct: this is $^{n}C_{r}$.
This is $^{n}P_{r}$, which counts ordered arrangements.
The (n − r)! for the objects left out is missing.
The n! in the numerator is missing; this is the denominator only.

explanation: Each selection of $r$ objects appears $r!$ times among the $^{n}P_{r}$ arrangements, so $^{n}C_{r} = \dfrac{^{n}P_{r}}{r!} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$.

stem: Evaluate $^{8}C_{3}$ without a calculator.
explanation: $^{8}C_{3} = \dfrac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = \dfrac{336}{6} = 56$.

stem: In how many ways can 3 learners be chosen from a class of 12 to represent the class at a meeting?
explanation: Order does not matter: $^{12}C_{3} = \dfrac{12 \times 11 \times 10}{6} = 220$.

stem: $^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{n-r}$ for $0 \leq r \leq n$.
explanation: Choosing the r objects to take is the same as choosing the n − r objects to leave behind.
They are equal: $^{10}C_{3} = {}^{10}C_{7} = 120$, because choosing 3 to take is the same as choosing 7 to leave.

stem: A coach chooses a cricket team of 11 from a squad of 15. Which calculation gives the number of possible teams?

options.rationale: Correct: $^{15}C_{11} = {}^{15}C_{4}$; choosing the 4 to leave out is quicker. Both equal 1365.
This counts ordered line-ups, but a team is a selection.
This does not count selections of 11 people.
The players are chosen from 15, not from 11.

explanation: A team is a selection, so use combinations: $^{15}C_{11} = {}^{15}C_{4} = \dfrac{15 \times 14 \times 13 \times 12}{24} = 1365$.

stem: A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 teachers and 7 learners. How many different committees contain exactly 2 teachers?
explanation: 2 teachers from 5 and 2 learners from 7: $^{5}C_{2} \times {}^{7}C_{2} = 10 \times 21 = 210$.
hints: Choose the teachers and the learners separately.
Multiply, because both choices are made.

stem: A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 teachers and 7 learners. How many committees contain at least one teacher?
explanation: Total $^{12}C_{4} = 495$. With no teachers: $^{7}C_{4} = 35$. At least one teacher: $495 - 35 = 460$.
workedSolution: 1. Total $^{12}C_{4} = 495$. With no teachers: $^{7}C_{4} = 35$. At least one teacher: $495 - 35 = 460$.

stem: A group of 4 is chosen from 6 teachers and 7 learners. How many groups contain at most one teacher?
hints: At most one means 0 teachers or 1 teacher.
Work out each case, then add.

stem: A group of 4 is chosen from 13 people, including Chipo and Sipho. How many groups include Chipo but not Sipho?
explanation: Put Chipo in and leave Sipho out. The other 3 members come from the remaining 11 people: $^{11}C_{3} = 165$.
workedSolution: 1. Put Chipo in and leave Sipho out. The other 3 members come from the remaining 11 people: $^{11}C_{3} = 165$.
hints: Remove Chipo and Sipho from the pool first.

stem: Find the value of $n$ for which $^{n}C_{3} = 4 \times {}^{n}C_{2}$.
explanation: $\dfrac{n(n - 1)(n - 2)}{6} = 4 \times \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}$. Divide both sides by $n(n - 1)$ (non-zero): $\dfrac{n - 2}{6} = 2$, so $n = 14$.
hints: Write both sides as products and cancel n(n − 1).

stem: Match each expression to its value.
At a meeting, each of 9 people shakes hands once with every other person. How many handshakes take place?

options.rationale: $9 \times 8$ counts every handshake twice (A with B and B with A).
Correct: each handshake is a pair of people, $^{9}C_{2} = 36$.
$9^{2}$ includes people shaking hands with themselves and counts pairs twice.
Each person shakes 8 hands, not 2.

explanation: A handshake is an unordered pair: $^{9}C_{2} = \dfrac{9 \times 8}{2} = 36$.
hints: Does the order of the two people in a handshake matter?

stem: Farai chooses 2 of 5 different maths revision books and 2 of 4 different science revision books. In how many ways can he choose his four books?

options.rationale: The choices have been added; both choices are made, so multiply.
$^{9}C_{4}$ ignores the condition of 2 from each subject.
This uses $^{5}P_{2} \times {}^{4}P_{2}$, but the order of choosing books does not matter.

explanation: Choose from each group separately and multiply: 10 ways for the maths books, 6 for the science books.
hints: Choose the maths books, then the science books.

stem: A farmer near Chinhoyi will plant 3 of 8 maize varieties and 2 of 5 bean varieties in a trial plot. How many different choices of varieties are possible?
hints: Both choices are made, so multiply.

stem: What is the most reliable way to count selections that contain at least one item from a group?

options.content: Choose one item from the group first, then choose the rest from everything left.
options.rationale: This counts some selections more than once (once for each group member they contain).

options.content: Multiply the size of the group by the total number of selections.
options.rationale: This has no counting meaning here.

options.content: Count all selections, then subtract those with none from the group.
options.rationale: Correct: every selection either has none or at least one, so the complement is quick and avoids double counting.

options.content: Count the selections with exactly one item from the group.
options.rationale: That misses the selections with two or more.

explanation: At least one = total − none. The direct method of choosing one first double counts.
hints: What is the opposite of at least one?

stem: Which of these is equal to $^{7}C_{2}$?

options.rationale: $^{7}C_{3} = 35$; the matching value is $^{7}C_{7-2}$.
Correct: choosing 2 to take is the same as choosing 5 to leave.

stem: A committee of 5 is to be chosen from 7 men and 6 women. Tendai is one of the men and Thandeka is one of the women.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many different committees can be chosen?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How many committees contain at least 3 women?

parts.label: (c)

parts.explanation: Committees with both: the other 3 from 11, $^{11}C_{3} = 165$. So $1287 - 165 = 1122$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Committees with both: the other 3 from 11, $^{11}C_{3} = 165$. So $1287 - 165 = 1122$.
